full_text: Abstract Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) joint inflammation remains poorly understood, despite its clinical burden. This review surveys in vitro joint models which were originally developed for arthritis research and examine how they can be repurposed to study CHIKV joint pathology. We outline key considerations, limitations, and recommendations for adapting these models for infection studies, including facilitating infection susceptibility across joint models, tuning matrix composition, addressing cellular incompleteness through modeling relevant immune cells, improving culture longevity and reproducibility. Together, these models offer versatile and human-relevant approaches to replicate key features of joint inflammation in advancing the understanding of CHIKV-induced joint pathology. Introduction Chikungunya virus (CHIKV), an arthritogenic alphavirus transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, has re-emerged as a significant global health concern. The World Health Organization reported a resurgence of CHIKV from 1 January to 30 September 2025, with 445,271 suspected/confirmed cases and 155 deaths across 40 countries; these cases spanned Africa, the Americas, South-East Asia, and the Western Pacific, and local transmission was reported in Europe1. Beyond the acute febrile illness, which is typically self-limiting and resolves within one to two weeks, a substantial proportion of CHIKV-infected patients develop persistent joint inflammation that can last for years post-acute infection2,3. This persistent joint pain, despite resolution of viremia, distinguishes CHIKV from other arboviral infections and underscores the importance of understanding its joint-specific pathology, particularly as the tissue-specific mechanisms driving persistence remain poorly defined. Although CHIKV-induced joint inflammation shares certain immunological features with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), there are important distinctions between the two (Fig. 1). Both conditions involve CD4+ T cell activation and elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines, and transcriptomic analyses in mouse models have revealed overlapping gene signatures related to T cell activation, antigen presentation, and innate and adaptive immune responses4,5,6,7. However, similarity in gene expression does not imply identical disease mechanisms. RA is driven by a breakdown in immune tolerance, leading to the production of autoantibodies such as anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPAs) and rheumatoid factor (RF), and is sustained by chronic CD4+ T cell activation with extensive crosstalk involving macrophages, dendritic cells, B cells, and fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS)5. In contrast, CHIKV-induced joint inflammation is initiated by viral infection, involves CD4+ T cells and macrophage interactions but lacks consistent autoantibody involvement, and is shaped by a chemokine-dominant profile (including CXCL8, CXCL9, and CXCL10) associated with antiviral responses8,9,10,11. While recent studies of CHIKV have primarily focused on systemic immune responses and macrophage-T cell interactions, it is likely that crosstalk between the resident cell types within the joint microenvironment, such as FLS, chondrocytes, and resident synovial macrophages, also contribute to CHIKV pathogenesis. These differences show that CHIKV-induced joint inflammation is a distinct pathophysiological process, and its mechanisms cannot be directly equated with those of autoimmune arthritides (Fig. 1). Despite its obvious clinical relevance, the joint remains underexplored in CHIKV research. Previous in vivo studies and analyses of patient serum have advanced our understanding of systemic immune responses, but they offer only a partial view of the disease mechanisms. Complex interactions between immune cells, stromal cells, and extracellular matrix (ECM) components in the joint microenvironment may drive CHIKV-induced pathology and its potential persistence. Sophisticated joint-focused experimental systems are therefore required for dissecting the underlying tissue-specific processes, such as those established in the field of RA and osteoarthritis (OA). While OA is a progressive age-related degenerative disorder, CHIKV-associated joint inflammation is typically self-limiting, but can become chronic in a subset of patients. Despite these differences, OA-based models can provide a relevant platform to investigate inflammation-driven matrix degradation and chondrocyte dysfunction. While several arthritogenic alphaviruses, including RRV, ONNV, and MAYV, can also cause joint inflammation and present with persistent arthralgia, the depth of clinical and mechanistic understanding varies across these infections12. CHIKV has been extensively characterized, with a rich body of clinical and emerging tissue-level evidence. However, long-term and mechanistic data for other alphaviruses remain limited. The extent to which underlying pathogenic mechanisms are shared across these viruses remains poorly defined and reflect differences in available evidence rather than true biological divergence. To contextualize CHIKV within the broader group of arthritogenic alphaviruses, a comparative summary is provided (Table 1), highlighting differences in clinical presentation and depth of current mechanism. As such, while in vitro joint models are broadly applicable across arthritogenic alphaviruses, this review focuses on CHIKV as a representative system with a more established evidence base. This review explores the ways in which experimental models originally developed for arthritis research can also be used to advance our understanding of CHIKV-induced joint pathology, drawing on tools such as two- and three-dimensional (2D and 3D) cell cultures, co-culture systems, and microfluidic joint-on-chip (JoC) platforms to interrogate viral-host interactions in a controlled, human-relevant context. This review was conducted as a narrative synthesis of the literature, with a focus on studies relevant to chikungunya virus-associated joint pathology and emerging joint models. Relevant articles were identified through searches of databases including PubMed, Web of Science, and Google Scholar using combinations of keywords such as “chikungunya virus”, “cartilage”, “synovial macrophages”, “fibroblastic-like synoviocytes”, and “joint models”. Rather than applying strict inclusion or exclusion criteria, studies were selected based on their relevance to the central themes of this review, with an emphasis on recent advances and mechanistic insights in CHIKV-associated joint pathology and joint modeling approaches. CHIKV-induced joint pathology To understand CHIKV joint pathology, it is important to consider the joint microenvironment, which provides the structural and biological context within which viral replication and immune activation occur. Firstly, the articular cartilage is an avascular and alymphatic tissue that lines the ends of bones within a joint and is composed primarily of chondrocytes embedded within an abundant ECM, allowing smooth articulation and absorbing load13. The surrounding synovial membrane lines the inner surface of the joint capsule and contains two main synoviocyte populations: type A macrophage-like synoviocytes, which function as phagocytic cells that clear debris and immune complexes, and type B FLS, which synthesize hyaluronan and lubricin to maintain joint lubrication and homeostasis14. Both synoviocytes and articular chondrocytes are immunologically active, capable of sensing pathogen- or damage-associated molecular patterns through pattern recognition receptors and responding via production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines15. The synovial membrane also produces synovial fluid, which fills the joint cavity and facilitates lubrication and nutrient and oxygen delivery to the avascular cartilage while serving as a reservoir for soluble mediators16. This tightly integrated joint microenvironment is highly susceptible to inflammatory disruption. The immunopathology of CHIKV infection has been extensively attributed to systemic immune responses, with CD4+ T cells playing a central role in driving joint inflammation and tissue damage. In mouse models, early studies demonstrated that depletion of CD4+ T cells significantly reduced footpad swelling without affecting viral load, indicating an inflammatory rather than antiviral functionality during CHIKV infection6. Within the joint-footpad, activated CD64+MHCII+ macrophages have been identified and shown to engage in pathogenic interactions with CD4+ T cells, contributing to local immunopathology through the secretion of inflammatory mediators (Fig. 2A)8. Complementing these murine findings, recent human blood studies have demonstrated that CHIKV-specific CD4+ T cells persist long after acute infection, predominantly produce TNF-α, implicating them in the maintenance of post-viral inflammation17. Viral antigen was also detected in the synovial biopsies (specifically, in synovial macrophages) of a CHIKV patient 18 months after the initial clinic visit18. In addition, CHIKV was also detected in joint tissues of non-human primates for up to 3 months post infection, raising the possibility of viral persistence19. Several studies have examined the roles of resident cell populations in CHIKV-induced joint pathology. Type B FLS or synovial fibroblasts are one of the main components in the joint microenvironment. Primary human FLS were susceptible to CHIKV replication in vitro, producing high viral titers of 105–106 pfu/ml and displaying cytopathic effects within days of infection20. Upon CHIKV infection, FLS predominantly secreted RANKL, IL-6, IL-8, and MCP-1, which recruited monocytes and drove their differentiation toward osteoclast-like cells (Fig. 2B). Notably, FLS were not major sources of TNF-α, IL-1β, or MMP-1, -2, or -13, which are known to induce arthritis. Instead, the resulting osteoclast-like cells contributed to bone resorption and secreted inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6, which exacerbated joint inflammation in vitro. This indicates that FLS are not direct mediators of joint destruction but instead act as initiators of an erosive cascade towards osteoclastogenesis. Single-cell transcriptomics have further implicated FLS as central effectors of CHIKV arthritis, highlighting their role in immune cell recruitment and RANKL-driven osteoclastogenesis21. Concordantly, proteomic profiling has demonstrated that CHIKV infection rapidly remodels the FLS proteome within 12 and 24 h post-infection, altering cellular trafficking and cytoskeletal, metabolic, and immune pathways in ways that may facilitate both viral replication and pro-inflammatory programming22. Finally, primary human FLS exhibited a miRNA-mediated dampening of innate signaling during CHIKV infection, with microarray profiling identifying approximately 26 host miRNAs predicted to target AKT3, TRIM26, SOCS7, and PELI1, consistent with suppression of the JAK-STAT, TLR, TNF, and NF-κB pathways that could favor viral persistence. Functionally, CHIKV upregulates miR-146a in human FLS, which downregulates TRAF6 and IRAK1/2, blunting NF-κB and thereby enhancing replication while modulating fibroblast inflammatory output23. Collectively, these findings identify FLS as pivotal amplifiers linking stromal infection to immune recruitment and joint damage. The role of type A macrophage-like synoviocytes (also called resident synovial macrophages) in CHIKV infection is less clear. Unlike the infiltrating monocyte-derived macrophages that dominate inflammatory settings, type A macrophages originate from embryonic precursors such as the yolk sac or fetal liver, and they are self-renewing and M2-like24. These macrophages were characterized as a unique CX3CR1+ tissue-resident population and known to establish a protective barrier at the synovial interface, where they limit immune cell entry via tight junctions, actively resolve inflammation through neutrophil clearance, and sustain homeostatic balance within the synovial microenvironment25,26. Their position at the synovial interface places these resident/barrier macrophages at a critical juncture between stromal integrity and viral pathogenesis, but whether they function as antigen-presenting sentinels or serve as potential reservoirs of persistence in the context of CHIKV infection is not yet known. Their roles remain largely unexplored due to the difficulty of isolating resident synovial macrophages, and most studies to date have relied on monocytic models such as THP-1 or U937 cell lines27,28,29. Very recently, chondrocytes were found to be permissive targets of CHIKV, whereby supporting viral replication and producing infectious virus30. Using a NanoLuc-expressing CHIKV, robust viral replication within the articular cartilage of immunocompetent mice was observed, with signals localizing to chondrocyte-rich regions. Histopathology confirmed infected chondrocytes with focal cartilage erosion and periarticular inflammation in mice. In vitro primary human chondrocytes were also productively infected, released infectious progeny, and underwent apoptosis. Infection also induced expression of MMP-3 and MMP-9, enzymes linked to proteoglycan and gelatin degradation, thereby coupling viral cytopathology with catabolic matrix remodeling (Fig. 2C). A CHIKV-infected 3D chondrocyte model cultured from patient joint samples also showed productive viral replication. Quantitative proteomics revealed strong interferon antiviral responses and broad remodeling of ubiquitination, phosphorylation, and metabolism, changes that were not found in matched 2D monolayers31. Taken together, these data established human chondrocytes as active participants in antiviral signaling and demonstrated that matrix context shapes virus-host interactions. Although evidence for CHIKV infection of chondrocytes is still emerging, it is supported by broader observations of joint tissue tropism across other arthritogenic alphaviruses, including Ross River Virus (RRV) and Mayaro virus (MAYV)32,33. Meanwhile, osteoblasts have also been identified as stromal targets of CHIKV infection. Infection of primary human osteoblasts supports viral replication and elicits robust secretion of IL-6 and RANKL, accompanied by reduced osteoprotegerin (OPG), thereby shifting the RANKL/OPG axis toward osteoclastogenesis and bone resorption (Fig. 2-D)34. The same cytokine imbalance was observed in the plasma of infected individuals, suggesting that the source of these mediators is osteoblasts35. While definitive in vivo validation is still lacking for CHIKV, comparable work in RRV has shown infected osteoblasts to display the same IL-6 and RANKL/OPG profiles. In murine models, this translates to bone loss measurable by micro-CT, with IL-6 neutralization attenuating osteoclast recruitment and preserving bone volume36. Importantly, this osteoblast program overlaps with observations from RA, where dysregulated RANKL/OPG signaling also fuels osteoclastogenesis and subchondral erosion37,38. Thus, in alphavirus arthritis, osteoblast infection adds a bone remodeling axis that complements synoviocyte-driven immune recruitment and chondrocyte-mediated matrix degradation. CHIKV-associated joint pathology is likely driven by multiple, non-mutually exclusive mechanisms. Among these, contributions from adaptive immune responses are relatively well supported. In contrast, several additional mechanisms have been proposed but remain poorly defined, including sustained activation and reprogramming of joint-resident stromal cells, persistence of replicating virus in tissue reservoirs, and retention of viral antigens in the absence of active replication. In this review, we adopt a framework in which persistent inflammation is primarily sustained by stromal–immune interactions following the acute phase, with viral or antigen persistence acting as potential initiating or amplifying factors. While evidence for long-term productive viral replication in joint tissues remains unclear, the presence of viral RNA or antigen and its role in local immune activation remains an area of ongoing investigation. full_text_sections.full_text: Abstract Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) joint inflammation remains poorly understood, despite its clinical burden. This review surveys in vitro joint models which were originally developed for arthritis research and examine how they can be repurposed to study CHIKV joint pathology. We outline key considerations, limitations, and recommendations for adapting these models for infection studies, including facilitating infection susceptibility across joint models, tuning matrix composition, addressing cellular incompleteness through modeling relevant immune cells, improving culture longevity and reproducibility. Together, these models offer versatile and human-relevant approaches to replicate key features of joint inflammation in advancing the understanding of CHIKV-induced joint pathology. Introduction Chikungunya virus (CHIKV), an arthritogenic alphavirus transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, has re-emerged as a significant global health concern. The World Health Organization reported a resurgence of CHIKV from 1 January to 30 September 2025, with 445,271 suspected/confirmed cases and 155 deaths across 40 countries; these cases spanned Africa, the Americas, South-East Asia, and the Western Pacific, and local transmission was reported in Europe1. Beyond the acute febrile illness, which is typically self-limiting and resolves within one to two weeks, a substantial proportion of CHIKV-infected patients develop persistent joint inflammation that can last for years post-acute infection2,3. This persistent joint pain, despite resolution of viremia, distinguishes CHIKV from other arboviral infections and underscores the importance of understanding its joint-specific pathology, particularly as the tissue-specific mechanisms driving persistence remain poorly defined. Although CHIKV-induced joint inflammation shares certain immunological features with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), there are important distinctions between the two (Fig. 1). Both conditions involve CD4+ T cell activation and elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines, and transcriptomic analyses in mouse models have revealed overlapping gene signatures related to T cell activation, antigen presentation, and innate and adaptive immune responses4,5,6,7. However, similarity in gene expression does not imply identical disease mechanisms. RA is driven by a breakdown in immune tolerance, leading to the production of autoantibodies such as anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPAs) and rheumatoid factor (RF), and is sustained by chronic CD4+ T cell activation with extensive crosstalk involving macrophages, dendritic cells, B cells, and fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS)5. In contrast, CHIKV-induced joint inflammation is initiated by viral infection, involves CD4+ T cells and macrophage interactions but lacks consistent autoantibody involvement, and is shaped by a chemokine-dominant profile (including CXCL8, CXCL9, and CXCL10) associated with antiviral responses8,9,10,11. While recent studies of CHIKV have primarily focused on systemic immune responses and macrophage-T cell interactions, it is likely that crosstalk between the resident cell types within the joint microenvironment, such as FLS, chondrocytes, and resident synovial macrophages, also contribute to CHIKV pathogenesis. These differences show that CHIKV-induced joint inflammation is a distinct pathophysiological process, and its mechanisms cannot be directly equated with those of autoimmune arthritides (Fig. 1). Despite its obvious clinical relevance, the joint remains underexplored in CHIKV research. Previous in vivo studies and analyses of patient serum have advanced our understanding of systemic immune responses, but they offer only a partial view of the disease mechanisms. Complex interactions between immune cells, stromal cells, and extracellular matrix (ECM) components in the joint microenvironment may drive CHIKV-induced pathology and its potential persistence. Sophisticated joint-focused experimental systems are therefore required for dissecting the underlying tissue-specific processes, such as those established in the field of RA and osteoarthritis (OA). While OA is a progressive age-related degenerative disorder, CHIKV-associated joint inflammation is typically self-limiting, but can become chronic in a subset of patients. Despite these differences, OA-based models can provide a relevant platform to investigate inflammation-driven matrix degradation and chondrocyte dysfunction. While several arthritogenic alphaviruses, including RRV, ONNV, and MAYV, can also cause joint inflammation and present with persistent arthralgia, the depth of clinical and mechanistic understanding varies across these infections12. CHIKV has been extensively characterized, with a rich body of clinical and emerging tissue-level evidence. However, long-term and mechanistic data for other alphaviruses remain limited. The extent to which underlying pathogenic mechanisms are shared across these viruses remains poorly defined and reflect differences in available evidence rather than true biological divergence. To contextualize CHIKV within the broader group of arthritogenic alphaviruses, a comparative summary is provided (Table 1), highlighting differences in clinical presentation and depth of current mechanism. As such, while in vitro joint models are broadly applicable across arthritogenic alphaviruses, this review focuses on CHIKV as a representative system with a more established evidence base. This review explores the ways in which experimental models originally developed for arthritis research can also be used to advance our understanding of CHIKV-induced joint pathology, drawing on tools such as two- and three-dimensional (2D and 3D) cell cultures, co-culture systems, and microfluidic joint-on-chip (JoC) platforms to interrogate viral-host interactions in a controlled, human-relevant context. This review was conducted as a narrative synthesis of the literature, with a focus on studies relevant to chikungunya virus-associated joint pathology and emerging joint models. Relevant articles were identified through searches of databases including PubMed, Web of Science, and Google Scholar using combinations of keywords such as “chikungunya virus”, “cartilage”, “synovial macrophages”, “fibroblastic-like synoviocytes”, and “joint models”. Rather than applying strict inclusion or exclusion criteria, studies were selected based on their relevance to the central themes of this review, with an emphasis on recent advances and mechanistic insights in CHIKV-associated joint pathology and joint modeling approaches. CHIKV-induced joint pathology To understand CHIKV joint pathology, it is important to consider the joint microenvironment, which provides the structural and biological context within which viral replication and immune activation occur. Firstly, the articular cartilage is an avascular and alymphatic tissue that lines the ends of bones within a joint and is composed primarily of chondrocytes embedded within an abundant ECM, allowing smooth articulation and absorbing load13. The surrounding synovial membrane lines the inner surface of the joint capsule and contains two main synoviocyte populations: type A macrophage-like synoviocytes, which function as phagocytic cells that clear debris and immune complexes, and type B FLS, which synthesize hyaluronan and lubricin to maintain joint lubrication and homeostasis14. Both synoviocytes and articular chondrocytes are immunologically active, capable of sensing pathogen- or damage-associated molecular patterns through pattern recognition receptors and responding via production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines15. The synovial membrane also produces synovial fluid, which fills the joint cavity and facilitates lubrication and nutrient and oxygen delivery to the avascular cartilage while serving as a reservoir for soluble mediators16. analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) joint inflammation, specifically examining arthritis models originally developed for arthritis research and how they can be repurposed to study CHIKV-induced joint pathology. The central question is how these models can be adapted to better understand the mechanisms of CHIKV joint inflammation, particularly its distinct pathophysiology compared to autoimmune conditions.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review is a narrative analysis of in vitro joint models, with no explicit mention of systematic search methods, databases, or meta-analysis. It outlines key considerations for adapting these models, including infection susceptibility, matrix composition, immune cell modeling, and culture longevity and reproducibility.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The review concludes that in vitro joint models provide versatile and human-relevant approaches to replicate key features of CHIKV-induced joint inflammation. These models are useful for studying the interactions between immune cells, stromal cells, and the extracellular matrix (ECM) in the joint microenvironment, which are critical for understanding CHIKV pathogenesis.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review highlights that while CHIKV-induced joint inflammation shares some immunological features with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), such as CD4+ T cell activation and pro-inflammatory cytokines, the mechanisms driving persistence remain poorly defined. Additionally, the joint microenvironment's complex interactions are underexplored in CHIKV research, and there is a lack of comprehensive studies on the role of resident cell types like fibroblast-like synoviocytes (FLS) and synovial macrophages.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review suggests that future research should focus on developing more sophisticated in vitro joint models that incorporate relevant immune cells and ECM components to better replicate the joint-specific pathology of CHIKV. It also emphasizes the need for studies that explore the role of crosstalk between joint-resident cells in CHIKV pathogenesis.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores arthritis models originally developed for arthritis research and their potential to study Chikungunya virus (CHIKV)-induced joint inflammation. It highlights the clinical burden of CHIKV, particularly its persistent joint pain, which distinguishes it from other arboviruses and autoimmune conditions like rheumatoid arthritis (RA). The review outlines key considerations for adapting these models, including infection susceptibility, matrix composition, and immune cell interactions. While some immunological features overlap with RA, CHIKV-induced joint inflammation is driven by distinct mechanisms, such as chemokine profiles and antiviral responses. The review identifies gaps in understanding the joint-specific pathophysiology of CHIKV and suggests future research directions to improve in vitro models for studying this condition.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 本综述聚焦于基孔肯雅病毒(CHIKV)引起的关节炎,具体探讨了最初为关节炎研究开发的模型以及它们如何被重新利用来研究CHIKV诱导的关节病理。核心问题是这些模型如何被调整以更好地理解CHIKV关节炎的机制,特别是其与自身免疫性疾病相比独特的病理生理学特征。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 本综述是对体外关节模型的叙述性分析,没有明确提及系统搜索方法、数据库或元分析。它概述了将这些模型进行调整的关键考虑因素,包括感染易感性、基质组成、免疫细胞建模以及培养的持续时间和可重复性。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 综述得出结论,体外关节模型提供了灵活且与人类相关的途径,以复制CHIKV诱导的关节炎的关键特征。这些模型有助于研究关节微环境中免疫细胞、基质细胞和细胞外基质(ECM)之间的相互作用,这对于理解CHIKV 发病机制至关重要。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 综述指出,尽管CHIKV引起的关节炎在某些免疫学特征上与类风湿性关节炎(RA)相似,例如CD4+ T细胞激活和促炎细胞因子,但驱动其持续性的机制仍不明确。此外,CHIKV研究中对关节微环境复杂相互作用的探索仍不足,缺乏对诸如成纤维细胞样滑膜细胞(FLS)和滑膜巨噬细胞等驻留细胞类型作用的全面研究。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 综述建议未来的研究应重点开发更复杂的体外关节模型,这些模型应包含相关免疫细胞和细胞外基质成分,以更准确地复制CHIKV的关节特异性病理。它还强调了需要研究关节驻留细胞之间相互作用在CHIKV 发病机制中的作用。

abstract_zh: 本综述调查了最初为关节炎研究开发的体外关节模型,并探讨了它们如何被重新利用来研究CHIKV引起的关节病理。因此,尽管体外关节模型在关节炎相关阿尔法病毒中具有广泛的应用性,但本综述重点聚焦于CHIKV作为具有更明确证据基础的代表性系统。本综述探讨了最初为关节炎研究开发的实验模型如何也能用于增进我们对CHIKV引起的关节病理的理解,利用诸如二维和三维(2D和3D)细胞培养、共培养系统以及微流控关节芯片(JoC)平台等工具,在可控且与人类相关的环境中研究病毒-宿主相互作用。本综述采用叙述性文献综合分析的方法,重点关注与基孔肯雅病毒相关关节病理以及新兴关节模型的研究。与应用严格的纳入或排除标准不同,研究的选择基于其与本综述核心主题的相关性,特别强调近期在CHIKV相关关节病理和关节建模方法上的进展和机制见解。尽管CHIKV引起的关节炎具有显著的临床负担,但其发病机制仍不明确。我们概述了在将这些模型用于感染研究时的关键考虑因素、局限性及建议,包括促进关节模型的感染易感性、调整基质组成、通过建模相关免疫细胞解决细胞不完整性问题,以及提高培养的持续时间和可重复性。总体而言,这些模型提供了灵活且与人类相关的途径,以复制CHIKV诱导关节炎的关键特征,从而推进对相关机制的理解。

title: Public discourse on knowledge, attitudes, and practices toward dengue and chikungunya in China: a multi-platform social media infoveillance study, 2022–2026
abstract: Dengue and chikungunya are expanding mosquito-borne arboviral diseases. In 2025, Guangdong (Foshan), China, experienced the largest domestic chikungunya outbreak on record. Real-world Chinese public discourse remains poorly characterised, and domestic KAP survey evidence is sparse and localised. We used social-media infoveillance to characterise Chinese public discourse on dengue and chikungunya across five platforms (2022–2026). We conducted an observational, cross-sectional infoveillance study. Public Chinese-language posts, comments, and danmaku mentioning dengue, chikungunya, or their vector were collected from Bilibili, Weibo, and Zhihu (API-based) and, because of platform anti-automation controls, Douyin and Xiaohongshu (manually extracted; n = 97, reported descriptively). After deduplication and relevance filtering, 4,707 records (4,610 API-collected) formed the analytic sample. We applied rule-based disease classification, a lexicon-based multi-label KAP-aligned thematic classifier (six themes), SnowNLP sentiment, a regex-screen plus adjudicated misinformation workflow, and a stratified qualitative subsample of long-form posts (n = 53). Classifier reliability was quantified against blinded human coding (N = 250). Multi-platform incremental value was assessed by active-month coverage. Chikungunya-focused content (38.5%) exceeded dengue-focused (25.9%); discourse spiked in July–August 2025 (n = 1,166 and 987), coinciding with the Guangdong outbreak. Transmission-route (33.8%) and preventive-practice (17.8%) themes dominated, whereas vaccine/treatment knowledge was thinnest (7.5%). Sentiment (n = 3,571) was near-balanced negative 40.9% / positive 40.6% / neutral 18.4%; disease focus was a significant but weak predictor (χ2 = 24.2, p < 0.001, Cramér's V = 0.058). The automated KAP classifier showed weak-to-moderate reliability (macro κ = 0.24; preventive-practice κ = 0.09, CI including zero; disease κ = 0.93). Misinformation was rare (3.47 per 1,000 records); the person-to-person myth yielded zero assertions, conspiracy-origin had the highest yield (27.8%), and corrective content rose during the outbreak while misinformation did not. Daily social-media volume peaked on 28 July 2025, ~ 7–9 days after the official case peak (19 July 2025), providing no advance warning. Multi-platform coverage: the three API platforms' active-month union was 51 months, but Weibo alone would have missed 31. Chinese public discourse on dengue and chikungunya is strongly outbreak-driven, prevention-oriented, and shows an affective valence near-balanced between negative vigilance and positive reassurance. The 2025 Guangdong outbreak exposed persistent discourse gaps, especially around vaccine/treatment reality and disease differentiation, that warrant proactive, video-first, multi-platform health communication. Social-media infoveillance is a useful complementary outbreak-intelligence component, but in this outbreak it tracked rather than preceded the clinical peak; multi-platform design materially outperformed any single platform. What is already known about this subject • Dengue is a long-established mosquito-borne disease in southern China, but chikungunya had not caused a substantial domestic outbreak on the mainland until the 2025 Guangdong/Foshan event, the largest chikungunya outbreak ever recorded in mainland China. • Surveys show that public knowledge of arboviral diseases is uneven, yet real-world public discourse on Chinese social media has not been systematically characterised for either dengue or chikungunya. • Social-media infoveillance is an established early-warning and health-communication tool, but most Chinese-platform studies focus on a single platform or a single disease. What this study adds • A five-platform (Bilibili, Weibo, Zhihu, Douyin, Xiaohongshu), 4,707-record infoveillance dataset spanning 2022–2026 shows that public attention shifted sharply toward chikungunya during the 2025 outbreak (38.5% of disease-focused posts vs 25.9% for dengue), with a clear monthly spike in July–August 2025 that mirrors the official Guangdong epidemic curve. • A KAP-framed discourse analysis shows that the vaccine/treatment theme is the thinnest discourse strand (7.6%). This fits the absence of a domestically available chikungunya vaccine and exposes a discourse gap (a potential communication blind spot) for risk communication. • Sentiment was near-balanced (negative 40.9% vs positive 40.6%), and short-video platforms (Bilibili science videos exceeding one million views) functioned as the dominant knowledge carrier, so outbreak communication should be video-first and proactively address the "no vaccine / symptomatic treatment only" message. • Multi-platform, real-world evidence: 4,707 cleaned Chinese social-media records (2022–2026) provide the first cross-platform characterisation of public discourse on knowledge, attitudes, and practices toward dengue and chikungunya in China. • Outbreak signal validity: The July–August 2025 chikungunya attention spike on social media tracks the official Guangdong/Foshan epidemic curve, supporting social media as a near-real-time outbreak-surveillance signal. • Identified discourse gap: Vaccine/treatment discourse was the weakest theme (7.6%), reflecting the lack of a domestic chikungunya vaccine and pointing to a clear health-communication target. • Platform role: Short-video content (e.g., Bilibili explainer videos with >1 million views) was the main knowledge channel, arguing for video-first, proactive public-health messaging during arboviral outbreaks. • Methodological transparency: The study openly reports platform anti-automation constraints (Douyin/Xiaohongshu collected via manual extraction as exploratory supplements) and follows ROSES + STROBE reporting.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 登革热和基孔肯雅热是正在扩展的蚊媒虫媒病毒病。2025年,中国广东省(佛山)经历了有记录以来最大的本土基孔肯雅病毒暴发。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 我们进行了一项观察性、横断面的监测研究。在去重和筛选相关记录后,形成了4,707条记录(其中4,610条来自API收集)的分析样本。以基孔肯雅热为中心的内容(38.5%)超过了以登革热为中心的内容(25.9%);讨论在2025年7月至8月期间激增(n = 1,166和987),与广东暴发同时发生。
elements_zh.methods: 我们利用社交媒体信息监测,对2022年至2026年间五个平台上关于登革热和基孔肯雅热的中国公众讨论进行了特征分析。我们应用了基于规则的疾病分类方法,一个基于词典的多标签KAP对齐主题分类器(六个主题),SnowNLP情感分析,一个结合正则表达式筛选和人工裁定的虚假信息处理流程,以及一个分层的定性子样本(n = 53),用于分析长文本帖子。分类器的可靠性通过与盲审的人类编码(N = 250)进行量化评估。
elements_zh.main_results: 从Bilibili、Weibo和Zhihu(基于API)收集了涉及登革热、基孔肯雅热或其媒介的中文公共帖子、评论和弹幕,由于平台的反自动化控制,抖音和小红书的数据(n = 97)是手动提取的,并以描述性方式报告。自动化的KAP分类器显示弱到中等的可靠性(宏观κ = 0.24;预防措施κ = 0.09,置信区间包含零;疾病κ = 0.93)。错误信息很少(每1,000条记录3.47条);人传人谬误产生了零条声明,阴谋论来源的错误信息最多(27.8%),而在暴发期间纠正性内容上升,而错误信息没有增加。

elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 多平台、真实世界证据:4,707条清理后的中国社交媒体记录(2022–2026年)提供了中国公众对登革热和基孔肯雅热的知识、态度和行为的首次跨平台特征分析。社交媒体信息监测是有用的补充性暴发情报组件,但在此次暴发中,它追踪了而非先于临床高峰;多平台设计在性能上显著优于任何单一平台。

This fits the absence of a domestically available chikungunya vaccine and exposes a discourse gap (a potential communication blind spot) for risk communication. • Sentiment was near-balanced (negative 40.9% vs positive 40.6%), and short-video platforms (Bilibili science videos exceeding one million views) functioned as the dominant knowledge carrier, so outbreak communication should be video-first and proactively address the "no vaccine / symptomatic treatment only" message. • Multi-platform, real-world evidence: 4,707 cleaned Chinese social-media records (2022–2026) provide the first cross-platform characterisation of public discourse on knowledge, attitudes, and practices toward dengue and chikungunya in China. • Outbreak signal validity: The July–August 2025 chikungunya attention spike on social media tracks the official Guangdong/Foshan epidemic curve, supporting social media as a near-real-time outbreak-surveillance signal. • Identified discourse gap: Vaccine/treatment discourse was the weakest theme (7.6%), reflecting the lack of a domestic chikungunya vaccine and pointing to a clear health-communication target. • Platform role: Short-video content (e.g., Bilibili explainer videos with >1 million views) was the main knowledge channel, arguing for video-first, proactive public-health messaging during arboviral outbreaks. • Methodological transparency: The study openly reports platform anti-automation constraints (Douyin/Xiaohongshu collected via manual extraction as exploratory supplements) and follows ROSES + STROBE reporting.

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 登革热和基孔肯雅热是正在扩展的蚊媒虫媒病毒病。2025年,中国广东省(佛山)经历了有记录以来最大的本土基孔肯雅病毒暴发。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 我们进行了一项观察性、横断面的监测研究。在去重和筛选相关记录后,形成了4,707条记录(其中4,610条来自API收集)的分析样本。以基孔肯雅热为中心的内容(38.5%)超过了以登革热为中心的内容(25.9%);讨论在2025年7月至8月期间激增(n = 1,166和987),与广东暴发同时发生。
analysis_zh.methods: 我们利用社交媒体信息监测,对2022年至2026年间五个平台上关于登革热和基孔肯雅热的中国公众讨论进行了特征分析。我们应用了基于规则的疾病分类方法,一个基于词典的多标签KAP对齐主题分类器(六个主题),SnowNLP情感分析,一个结合正则表达式筛选和人工裁定的虚假信息处理流程,以及一个分层的定性子样本(n = 53),用于分析长文本帖子。分类器的可靠性通过与盲审的人类编码(N = 250)进行量化评估。
analysis_zh.main_results: 从Bilibili、Weibo和Zhihu(基于API)收集了涉及登革热、基孔肯雅热或其媒介的中文公共帖子、评论和弹幕,由于平台的反自动化控制,抖音和小红书的数据(n = 97)是手动提取的,并以描述性方式报告。自动化的KAP分类器显示弱到中等的可靠性(宏观κ = 0.24;预防措施κ = 0.09,置信区间包含零;疾病κ = 0.93)。错误信息很少(每1,000条记录3.47条);人传人谬误产生了零条声明,阴谋论来源的错误信息最多(27.8%),而在暴发期间纠正性内容上升,而错误信息没有增加。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 2025年广东暴发暴露出持续的讨论差距,尤其是在疫苗/治疗现实和疾病区分方面,这些差距需要采取主动的、以视频为主的、多平台的健康沟通策略。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 多平台、真实世界证据:4,707条清理后的中国社交媒体记录(2022–2026年)提供了中国公众对登革热和基孔肯雅热的知识、态度和行为的首次跨平台特征分析。社交媒体信息监测是有用的补充性暴发情报组件,但在此次暴发中,它追踪了而非先于临床高峰;多平台设计在性能上显著优于任何单一平台。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 多平台覆盖:三个API平台的活跃月数并集为51个月,但仅使用微博则会遗漏31个月。提供的证据未报告与研究普遍性或样本量相关的具体局限性。

full_text: Proteases from Bacillus licheniformis destroy Aedes aegypti larvae Ana Carolina Silva Universidade Federal de Lavras Ruth Celestina Condori Mamani Universidade Federal de Lavras Amanda do Carmo Alves Universidade Federal de Lavras Jhennifer Cristiana Souza Universidade Federal de Lavras Ludimila Vieira Fernandes Universidade Federal de Lavras Ingrid Marciano Alvarenga Universidade Federal de Lavras Joziana Muniz Paiva Barçante Universidade Federal de Lavras Pedro Henryque Castro Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais Grasielle D ́ Avila Pessoa Caldas Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais Filippe Elias Freitas Soares Universidade Federal de Lavras Short Report Keywords: Aedes aegypti, protease, biochemical control, larvicidal, toxicity Posted Date: September 23rd, 2026 DOI: https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10120306/v1 License:   This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. Read Full License Page 1/12 Additional Declarations: No competing interests reported. Page 2/12 Abstract Controlling the Aedes aegypti vector, which transmits arboviruses such as DENV (dengue), ZIKV (Zika), and CHIKV (chikungunya), represents a global challenge that requires the development of new biotechnological larvicides. This study evaluated the efficacy of a formulation containing proteases derived from Bacillus licheniformis at different concentrations (0.1%, 0.5%, 1.0%, and 1.5% w/v) on early third-instar larvae. Toxicity bioassays revealed a dose- and time-dependent larvicidal effect. In the first 24 hours, the highest concentration (1.5%) achieved 80% mortality, rising to 100% after 72 hours. In contrast, the control and denatured formulation groups remained viable, demonstrating that lethality is dependent on the enzymatic activity of the proteases (p < 0.05). Morphological analysis by light microscopy corroborated the quantitative data, revealing cuticular disintegration and leakage of visceral contents in larvae exposed to the highest doses, evidencing the tissue damage caused by the formulation. The results indicate that the protease derived from B. licheniformis tested has high potential as a fast-acting larvicide, presenting itself as an alternative for integrated vector management strategies. Introduction Aedes aegypti is a mosquito of enormous public health importance, as it serves as the primary vector for arboviruses such as DENV, ZIKV, and CHIKV, which affect millions of people annually, especially in tropical and subtropical regions. The wide geographic distribution of this insect, combined with its high adaptive capacity and ability to thrive in urban environments, contributes to the recurring increase in epidemic outbreaks and to the difficulty in controlling the vector population. Thus, effective and sustainable strategies for reducing larval populations are essential to minimize the transmission of these arboviruses (Serdeiro et al., 2023, Vasantha-Srinivasan et al.,2024). Chemical control, based primarily on the use of synthetic larvicides, has been widely employed as a method to combat the mosquito. However, the use of chemical agents can cause environmental impacts, toxicity to non-target organisms, and, most importantly, the development of resistance by natural insect populations (Zulfa et al., 2022). Given these limitations, there is growing interest in biotechnological and biological alternatives that offer greater selectivity and lower ecological risk, as they are considered more suitable for integrated vector control programs (Sengul Demirak and Canpolat, 2022). Among the alternative methods for controlling A. aegypti, metabolites produced by microorganisms— particularly bacteria of the genus Bacillus—stand out for their ability to synthesize bioactive compounds and hydrolytic enzymes with insecticidal potential (Falqueto et al., 2021). In this context, formulations based on Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis (Bti) have been widely used for larval control, acting through crystalline toxins (Cry, Cyt1Aa) that promote the lysis of intestinal epithelial cells after ingestion (Brühl et al.,2020; Menezes et al.,2025). Although Bti-based formulations are widely used in the biological control of A. aegypti due to their high efficacy, the development of cell-free biotechnology products has broadened the prospects for larval Page 3/12 control. The application of Bti-based products relies on the use of spores and protein crystals, whose stability and performance can be influenced by environmental and operational factors (Brühl et al., 2020). In contrast, enzymatic formulations composed of purified biomolecules do not require the release of viable microorganisms into the environment, which can simplify aspects related to production, formulation, and application. Furthermore, the mechanism of action of Bti is associated with the ingestion and activation of toxins in the larvae’s gut (Brühl et al., 2020; Menezes et al., 2025), whereas exogenous bacterial proteases have the potential to act on different biological structures, including the cuticle and the peritrophic matrix (Nimbulkar et al., 2025). This characteristic suggests a multi-target action, capable of compromising the insect’s physical and physiological barriers, as well as enhancing the penetration and efficacy of other biological control agents when used in combined strategies. In this scenario, the present study evaluated the larvicidal efficacy of a commercial formulation of B. licheniformis proteases, at different concentrations, against third-instar (L3) larvae of A. aegypti. Larval mortality was evaluated over a period of 72 h. Additionally, the stability of the formulation’s proteolytic activity was investigated under conditions similar to those of the bioassay. Materials and Methods Obtaining and maintaining Aedes aegypti Aedes aegypti (Rockefeller strain) were obtained from the colony maintained at the Parasitic Biology Laboratory II (Department of Medicine, Federal University of Lavras). The females were fed with hamsters, in accordance with the protocol approved by the Animal Ethics Committee (CEUA) of the UFLA Office of the Vice-Rector for Research (No. 026/21). The eggs were incubated in 1.5 L of dechlorinated tap water in rectangular plastic containers with lids (40 × 12 × 12 cm). The larvae were fed crushed fish feed and maintained at 25 ± 2°C under a 12:12 h photoperiod (light:dark). After five days, third-stage (L3) larvae were obtained and used in the bioassays. Obtaining the enzyme The commercial formulation of B. licheniformis proteases (HPF) was kindly provided by Prozyn® (São Paulo, Brazil). Stability of the enzyme formulation Proteolytic activity was measured using the caseinolytic assay (Braga et al., 2011). For this assay, a solution containing 0.5 mL of 1% (w/v) casein, 0.45 mL of 100 mM Tris-HCl buffer, pH 8, and 0.05 mL of the enzymatic formulation at 0.1% or 1.5% (w/v) were incubated at 50°C for 15 min in test tubes. After this time, the reaction was stopped by adding 1 mL of 10% (w/v) trichloroacetic acid (TCA). Immediately thereafter, the solutions were centrifuged at 10,000 g for 10 min. The supernatant was recovered for Page 4/12 measurement in a UV-Vis spectrophotometer at 280 nm. One enzyme unit was defined as the amount of protease required to release 1 μg of tyrosine per minute under test conditions. To evaluate the stability of the B. licheniformis protease formulation, proteolytic activity was measured at 24, 48 and 72 hours. A solution of the proteolytic product was prepared using dechlorinated tap water and subsequently incubated at 27 ± 1°C under the same conditions as the bioassay with the larvae. In vitro assay on Aedes aegypti larvae (L) A bioassay to evaluate the effect of B. licheniformis proteases on third-instar larvae of A. aegypti was conducted according to World Health Organization guidelines, with modifications. Six experimental groups were established: a control group containing only dechlorinated water (G1); a control group containing the denatured formulation (boiled for 2 hours) (G2); and four treatment groups: HPF (G3) (1.5% w/v), HPF (G4) (1% w/v), HPF (G5) (0.5% w/v), and HPF (G6) (0.1% w/v). For each experimental group, 50 mL of solution prepared in dechlorinated water and 30 third-instar (L3) larvae of A. aegypti were used. The assay was conducted in plastic cups (4.5 cm in diameter × 8.5 cm in height), with five replicates for each group, and was repeated three times on different days. Mortality was assessed over three days. Larvae were considered dead when they could not reach the surface of the solution upon shaking the cups, and also when they showed no signs of movement, even after being gently touched with a glass rod. If pupae formed, they were considered live larvae. All groups were incubated at 27 ± 1°C, and the larvae were fed daily (Falvo et al., 2018). Statistical Analysis The bioassay data were initially subjected to the Shapiro-Wilk and Bartlett tests to assess normality and homoscedasticity. Following this assessment, a one-way ANOVA was performed using BioEstat software version 5.3 to evaluate differences between treatment groups. When ANOVA indicated significant differences, Tukey’s test was applied for paired comparisons of means. The confidence interval was 99% (Ayres et al., 2003). The mean percentage of larval mortality (L3) was calculated using the equation below, described by Mendoza-De-Gives and Vazquez-Prats (Mendoza-De Gives and Vazquez-Prats, 1994). %Reduction = (Average of control − Average of treatment) × 100 Average of control Results Stability of the enzyme formulation Page 5/12 The stability of the B. licheniformis proteases was evaluated at the highest and lowest concentrations used in the bioassay (0.1% and 1.5%). The results are presented in Table 1. Table 1 Assessment of the stability of proteolytic activity (U/mL) in the protease formulation derived from Bacillus licheniformis (HPF), supplied by Prozyn®, under the same conditions as those used in the in vitro assay on Aedes aegypti larvae. Proteolytic activity (± U/mL) HPF concentration 24h 48h 72h 0.1% (w/v) 154.44(± 0.003) 150.16(± 0.004) 151.03(± 0.002) 1.5% (w/v) 204.88(± 0.011) 200.44(± 0.021) 189.51(± 0.018) In vitro assay on Aedes aegypti larvae (L) According to the results, dose-dependent and time-dependent larvicidal activity was observed (Fig. 1). The negative control group and the group containing the denatured formulation showed no mortality, maintaining 100% larval viability throughout the experiment, with no statistically significant difference between them (p > 0.05). In the first 24 hours, the highest concentration (1.5% (w/v)) caused 83.3% mortality, differing significantly from the control (p < 0.01), while the lowest concentration (0.1% (w/v)) resulted in 53.3% mortality. After 72 hours of exposure to the treatments, the efficacy of the 1.5% (w/v) formulation reached 100% mortality, while the 0.1% (w/v) concentration resulted in 83.3% larval mortality. Intra-period statistical analysis showed that, after 24 hours, the 1.0% and 1.5% (w/v) concentrations exhibited greater toxicity than the lower doses (p < 0.01). At the 48-hour and 72-hour time points, the mortality rate increased in all treated groups, with the 1.5% (w/v) dose being significantly more effective than the others (p < 0.05), except for the similarity observed among the higher doses in the final stages of the experiment (p > 0.05). Figure 2 illustrates the morphological changes caused by exposure to protease. It is noted that, at a concentration of 1.5% (w/v) (Fig. 2D), there is an extravasation of the visceral contents, evidencing the proteolytic effect of the formulation. Discussion The enzymatic formulation containing protease derived from B. licheniformis exhibited significant larvicidal activity against A. aegypti larvae (L3), with a dose-dependent pattern and an increasing mortality rate over time. The 83% mortality of larvae within the first 24 h at a concentration of 1.5% (w/v) and complete mortality within 72 h indicate that the enzyme acts rapidly and efficiently to compromise Page 6/12 larval survival. t is important to highlight that even the lowest concentration tested (0.1% w/v; 1 mg/mL) caused approximately 95% mortality after 72 hours. It indicates substantial biological activity at a concentration 15 times lower than that required to achieve complete mortality. This finding is relevant from an application standpoint, since high efficacy at low concentrations can reduce the demand for protease and improve the economic viability of large-scale production and field implementation. Furthermore, these results corroborate findings in the literature demonstrating that bacterial enzymes, especially chitinases and proteases, act on essential insect structures, such as the cuticle and the midgut epithelium, promoting the degradation of structural and digestive components, which leads to tissue lysis, physiological disorganization, and, consequently, the death of the organism (Mahathir et al., 2025 and Pineda and Castellanos-Rozo, 2025). Possible mechanisms of action of bacterial proteases on A. aegypti larvae are mainly associated with the degradation of the peritrophic matrix, a layer composed of chitin and glycoproteins that protects the intestinal epithelium of the insect or larva (Vasantha-Srinivasam et al., 2024). Proteolytic activity promotes the breakdown of this barrier, increasing permeability and exposing epithelial cells to direct damage. Additionally, these enzymes may interfere with the activity of digestive proteases such as trypsin and chymotrypsin, impairing digestion and nutrient absorption. As a result, there is disruption of the intestinal epithelium, nutritional deficiency, and physiological collapse, leading to the death of the larvae (Shamsi et al., 2018). The proteolytic activity observed in this study is consistent with the study by Katak et al., (2021), who used supernatants from different strains of Bacillus ssp. containing hydrolytic enzymes. These supernatants were lyophilized and dissolved in distilled water to a concentration of 5 mg/mL. This solution resulted in a 93% mortality rate among A. aegypti larvae after 72 hours of exposure. However, an important advantage of the present study is the use of a commercial enzymatic product (HPF) from B. licheniformis, which allows larval mortality to be attributed directly to proteolytic activity, eliminating the variability and combined effects of multiple metabolites present in bacterial supernatants (Fig. 2). It is important to note that the bioassays in this study were conducted using third-instar (L3) A. aegypti larvae, a stage in which individuals exhibit greater physiological robustness, a thicker cuticle, and more developed defense mechanisms compared to earlier stages (Farnesi et al., 2012). For this reason, the high mortality rates observed in L3 suggest that proteases are highly effective in later instars. In other words, it is expected that A. aegypti larvae in earlier instars (L1 and L2), which have thinner cuticles and lower detoxification capacity, will be even more susceptible to enzymatic action, possibly resulting in even faster and more pronounced mortality. A comparison with studies involving other bacteria that produce larvicidal enzymes, such as Pseudomonas putida and various species of Bacillus and Serratia, shows that the use of hydrolases such as proteases causes damage to the cuticle and digestive system, resulting in high mortality within the first 48–72 hours (Jupatanakul et al., 2020 and Mini and Mathew, 2023). Therefore, the results reinforce Page 7/12 that the proteases of B. licheniformis possess characteristics consistent with the efficacy patterns already reported for other bacterial species applied as biocontrol agents. The formulation used in this study maintained enzymatic activity for 72 h under the same conditions as the bioassay with the larvae. A relevant point to consider, given that enzymes tend to experience a reduction in enzymatic activity due to variations in temperature, pH, and contact with other organic and inorganic compounds (Nelson and Cox, 2017), is that the water used for the assay was dechlorinated tap water; that is, other elements were present in it, such as fluoride and calcium, among others. These data indicate the potential for practical use of these proteases, especially in domestic or peri-urban applications, where sustained activity is necessary to target heterogeneous larval populations over time. Finally, the results obtained demonstrate that the B. licheniformis protease is a promising alternative for the development of bioinsecticide formulations intended for the control of A. aegypti. In addition to exhibiting high stability in tap water throughout the experimental period, the enzyme evaluated achieved mortality rates of approximately 95% at a concentration of just 0.1% (w/v) after 72 hours of exposure, demonstrating its potential for effectiveness even at low concentrations. These characteristics, combined with the growing demand for more sustainable and environmentally safe control strategies, reinforce the potential of this technology for applications in vector management. However, before its large-scale implementation, additional studies are needed to evaluate its persistence under real-world field conditions, its interaction with organic matter and other environmental components, and possible synergistic effects with biological agents already used in mosquito control, as well as its stability and enzymatic activity under different environmental conditions. Page 2/12 Abstract Controlling the Aedes aegypti vector, which transmits arboviruses such as DENV (dengue), ZIKV (Zika), and CHIKV (chikungunya), represents a global challenge that requires the development of new biotechnological larvicides. This study evaluated the efficacy of a formulation containing proteases derived from Bacillus licheniformis at different concentrations (0.1%, 0.5%, 1.0%, and 1.5% w/v) on early third-instar larvae. Toxicity bioassays revealed a dose- and time-dependent larvicidal effect. In the first 24 hours, the highest concentration (1.5%) achieved 80% mortality, rising to 100% after 72 hours. In contrast, the control and denatured formulation groups remained viable, demonstrating that lethality is dependent on the enzymatic activity of the proteases (p < 0.05). Morphological analysis by light microscopy corroborated the quantitative data, revealing cuticular disintegration and leakage of visceral contents in larvae exposed to the highest doses, evidencing the tissue damage caused by the formulation. The results indicate that the protease derived from B. licheniformis tested has high potential as a fast-acting larvicide, presenting itself as an alternative for integrated vector management strategies. Introduction Aedes aegypti is a mosquito of enormous public health importance, as it serves as the primary vector for arboviruses such as DENV, ZIKV, and CHIKV, which affect millions of people annually, especially in tropical and subtropical regions. The wide geographic distribution of this insect, combined with its high adaptive capacity and ability to thrive in urban environments, contributes to the recurring increase in epidemic outbreaks and to the difficulty in controlling the vector population. Thus, effective and sustainable strategies for reducing larval populations are essential to minimize the transmission of these arboviruses (Serdeiro et al., 2023, Vasantha-Srinivasan et al.,2024). Chemical control, based primarily on the use of synthetic larvicides, has been widely employed as a method to combat the mosquito. However, the use of chemical agents can cause environmental impacts, toxicity to non-target organisms, and, most importantly, the development of resistance by natural insect populations (Zulfa et al., 2022). Given these limitations, there is growing interest in biotechnological and biological alternatives that offer greater selectivity and lower ecological risk, as they are considered more suitable for integrated vector control programs (Sengul Demirak and Canpolat, 2022). Among the alternative methods for controlling A. aegypti, metabolites produced by microorganisms— particularly bacteria of the genus Bacillus—stand out for their ability to synthesize bioactive compounds and hydrolytic enzymes with insecticidal potential (Falqueto et al., 2021). In this context, formulations based on Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis (Bti) have been widely used for larval control, acting through crystalline toxins (Cry, Cyt1Aa) that promote the lysis of intestinal epithelial cells after ingestion (Brühl et al.,2020; Menezes et al.,2025). Although Bti-based formulations are widely used in the biological control of A. aegypti due to their high efficacy, the development of cell-free biotechnology products has broadened the prospects for larval Page 3/12 control. The application of Bti-based products relies on the use of spores and protein crystals, whose stability and performance can be influenced by environmental and operational factors (Brühl et al., 2020). In contrast, enzymatic formulations composed of purified biomolecules do not require the release of viable microorganisms into the environment, which can simplify aspects related to production, formulation, and application. Furthermore, the mechanism of action of Bti is associated with the ingestion and activation of toxins in the larvae’s gut (Brühl et al., 2020; Menezes et al., 2025), whereas exogenous bacterial proteases have the potential to act on different biological structures, including the cuticle and the peritrophic matrix (Nimbulkar et al., 2025). This characteristic suggests a multi-target action, capable of compromising the insect’s physical and physiological barriers, as well as enhancing the penetration and efficacy of other biological control agents when used in combined strategies. In this scenario, the present study evaluated the larvicidal efficacy of a commercial formulation of B. licheniformis proteases, at different concentrations, against third-instar (L3) larvae of A. aegypti. Larval mortality was evaluated over a period of 72 h. Additionally, the stability of the formulation’s proteolytic activity was investigated under conditions similar to those of the bioassay. Materials and Methods Obtaining and maintaining Aedes aegypti Aedes aegypti (Rockefeller strain) were obtained from the colony maintained at the Parasitic Biology Laboratory II (Department of Medicine, Federal University of Lavras). The females were fed with hamsters, in accordance with the protocol approved by the Animal Ethics Committee (CEUA) of the UFLA Office of the Vice-Rector for Research (No. 026/21). The eggs were incubated in 1.5 L of dechlorinated tap water in rectangular plastic containers with lids (40 × 12 × 12 cm). The larvae were fed crushed fish feed and maintained at 25 ± 2°C under a 12:12 h photoperiod (light:dark). After five days, third-stage (L3) larvae were obtained and used in the bioassays. Obtaining the enzyme The commercial formulation of B. licheniformis proteases (HPF) was kindly provided by Prozyn® (São Paulo, Brazil). Stability of the enzyme formulation Proteolytic activity was measured using the caseinolytic assay (Braga et al., 2011). For this assay, a solution containing 0.5 mL of 1% (w/v) casein, 0.45 mL of 100 mM Tris-HCl buffer, pH 8, and 0.05 mL of the enzymatic formulation at 0.1% or 1.5% (w/v) were incubated at 50°C for 15 min in test tubes. After this time, the reaction was stopped by adding 1 mL of 10% (w/v) trichloroacetic acid (TCA). Immediately thereafter, the solutions were centrifuged at 10,000 g for 10 min. The supernatant was recovered for Page 4/12 measurement in a UV-Vis spectrophotometer at 280 nm. One enzyme unit was defined as the amount of protease required to release 1 μg of tyrosine per minute under test conditions. To evaluate the stability of the B. licheniformis protease formulation, proteolytic activity was measured at 24, 48 and 72 hours. A solution of the proteolytic product was prepared using dechlorinated tap water and subsequently incubated at 27 ± 1°C under the same conditions as the bioassay with the larvae. summary_zh: 摘要 控制传播登革热病毒(DENV)、寨卡病毒(ZIKV)和基孔肯雅病毒(CHIKV)等虫媒病毒的埃及伊蚊(Aedes aegypti)媒介是一项全球性挑战,需要开发新的生物技术杀幼虫剂。本研究评估了含有从利福尼亚芽孢杆菌(Bacillus licheniformis)提取的蛋白酶制剂在不同浓度(0.1%、0.5%、1.0%和1.5% w/v)下对早期第三龄幼虫的效果。毒性生物测定显示杀幼虫效果具有剂量和时间依赖性。在前24小时内,最高浓度(1.5%)达到80% 死亡率,72小时后升至100%。相比之下,对照组和变性制剂组的幼虫仍然存活,这表明致死性依赖于蛋白酶的酶活性(p < 0.05)。利福尼亚芽孢杆菌测试的蛋白酶具有作为快速作用杀幼虫剂的高潜力,为综合媒介管理策略提供了替代方案。
